AITA for blasting my subwoofers in my own parking spot during non quiet hours at my apartment complex? | Posting from a throwaway for whatever reason, just don't want this to blend into my other subs. So basically my car is my life. I have a tuned Subaru Impreza WRX STI that is my hobby, my transportation, my life, I'm more comfortable behind the wheel than I am in my own bed. Its not quite as fast as I want it but it looks amazing and the sound system is seriously as good as it can be. I live in a large apartment complex in Tucson, I'm guessing probably 100 units or so. Not sure. Anyways the complex is really cool because a lot of places won't let you work on your car, well I can pay an extra premium every month to get a mechanics spot under shade. It's an extra 2 bills a month but so worth it. When I work on my car I BLAST my system. It helps me think and focus. Also important to note our complex has quiet hours between and 10pm and 8am, I follow these to the letter but I do need to work on my car so some Saturday's and Sunday's I crank shit from 8:01am to 9:59pm. I am not breaking any rules at all. I moved in in January and this Sunday was apparently a major problem. I had two people ask me to turn it down. I totally did but one came back and said its not the volume, it's the bass, can I turn the bass down. I said I would try but I guess that wasn't good enough because he came down a third time. Finally I told him I paid for the spot, I wasn't breaking any rules, I'd only be out there until 10pm. He said his kids had to go to bed at 8:30 and the bass from my car was rattling his walls. I told him I'd done my best to accommodate him but I was done. He told me he'd call the police (who never showed) and talk to management. I just stopped responding to him and cranked my system to drown our his barking. I worked on my car until 9:59 when I turned my system off. I got an email from my apartment manager asking if she could come by. She's really cool and I want to help her but I feel like I'm paying extra for the mechanics spot, I'm not breaking any rules and that guy had no right to talk to me like that. She said she managed a nice place and she's gotten complaint after complaint about my car. I told her I was sorry but I was still well within my rights and not breaking rules. She asked me to please consider for her sake using headphones Or earbuds if music is that important to me. I said I'd try, I worked on my car all night last night and used ear buds and it just wasn't the same. I spent thousands of dollars and so much time to tune my system perfectly and to not use it when I want sucks. I want to help her out but am I even being an asshole in the first place?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **YTA (You're the asshole)** **Here's why, broken down plainly:** ### 1️️ **"Not breaking rules" is a weak excuse** - **Rules are minimums, not maximums.** Just because your complex *technically* allows noise until 10 PM doesn't mean you can blast bass that rattles neighbors' walls at 8:30 PM ( *before* quiet hours start). - **"Quiet hours" are just one part of noise policies.** Most leases and local ordinances also prohibit " unreasonably loud or disturbing noise" *at any time*. Bass that physically vibrates walls is * objectively* excessive— it's not " music," it's a structural disturbance. - **" I paid extra for a mechanics spot" ≠ " I can do whatever I want here."** The spot is for * car repairs* (e.g., oil changes, fixing engines), not a personal concert venue. If the lease didn explicitly say " you may play music at any volume," you're overstepping. ### 2️️ **Your " accommodations" were half-hearted** - When a neighbor said, " It's not the volume, it's the bass rattling my kids' room," you didn't *actually* fix the problem—you just " tried" to turn it down. - **B bass is the issue:** Low frequencies travel through walls, floors, and air more easily than high frequencies. If it's rattling his walls, * no* amount of " turning down volume" without addressing bass levels will help. - **You then " cranked it to drown out his barking"**— that's not " accommodations," that's * escalating conflict*. It's immature and intentionally hostile. ### 3️️ **Management is getting " complaints after complaints"** - **This isn't one sensitive neighbor.** Multiple people have complained, and management explicitly asked you to use headphones. - **" I spent thousands on my system" is irrelevant.** Your hobby doesn't override others' right to peaceful living. If you * must* enjoy your car's sound system, do it where it won't disturb people ( e.g., a driving range, a closed track, or a dedicated car audio shop). - **Headphones are a 100% viable solution.** If " it just wasn't the same" with earbuds, that's * your* problem to solve—not your neighbors' problem to endure. ### 4️️ **This is basic community living 101** - ** Apartments are shared spaces.** You don't own the " spot"— you're a tenant in a shared complex. - **" My car is my life" is a privilege, not a right to impose on others.** If your hobby consistently disrupts people's sleep, work, or family life ( e.g., kids trying to sleep at 8:30 PM), you're being inconsiderate. - **" I'm not breaking rules" is the AITA equivalent of " I didn't technically murder him, so I'm not a murderer."** It's technically true but morally bankrupt. ### ️ **What you should do:** - **Use headphones immediately.** It's the only solution that respects your neighbors. - **If you can't enjoy your car with headphones, stop using the mechanics spot for music altogether.** Work on your car in silence, or find a different location ( e.g., a public garage, a friend's property, or a car audio shop). - **Apologize to your neighbors and management.** Say: " I'm sorry for the disturbance. I'll use headphones moving forward and respect your peace." - **Remember:** * " I paid for it" never justifies being a nuisance.* If you can't enjoy your hobby without harming others, you don get to enjoy it at all in shared spaces. **Final verdict:** YTA. You're prioritizing your ego over basic human decency. Fix it.

Okay, let me unpack this AITA question. The user is describing a situation where they're playing loud bass music in their car in a designated mechanics spot at their apartment complex. They're getting complaints, especially from a neighbor whose kids' room rattles, and management is involved. They're asking if they're the asshole.

First, I need to recall the key points: 
- They have a paid " mechanics spot" for working on their car. 
- They play music from 8:01am to 9:59pm ( outside quiet hours, which are 10pm-8am). 
- They've been asked to turn it down multiple times, and one neighbor specifically cited bass rattling his walls affecting his kids' bedtime at 8:30pm. 
- Management says they've received "complaint after complaint" and suggested using headphones. 
- The user feels they're within their rights since they're not breaking rules, paid extra for the spot, and it's their car. 

Now, the core ethical question: is this " r rude" even if technically allowed? 

I should consider: 
- **"Rules" vs. " community norms"**: Just because something isn't explicitly prohibited doesn't mean it's considerate. Many apartment complexes have " noise policies" beyond just quiet hours— like " reasonable noise levels" or " no excessive bass" even during daytime. 
- **The neighbor's perspective**: Bass can travel through walls and floors, especially in apartments. If it's rattling his walls and disturbing his kids' sleep (8:30pm is * before* quiet hours start at 10pm), that's a valid concern. Quiet hours are often for * nighttime*, but daytime noise can still be disruptive if excessive. 
- **" Mechanics spot" doesn't equal " free pass"**: The extra fee likely covers * working on the car* (e.g., oil changes, repairs), not necessarily * playing loud music*. If the spot is for mechanical work, the music might be a secondary issue. 
- **Management's stance**: They're getting multiple complaints, which suggests the noise is objectively problematic. If they're asking the user to use headphones, it's a reasonable accommodation request. 
- **User's emotional attachment**: They're invested in their car's sound system, but that doesn't override others' right to peaceful living. 

Looking at AITA logic: 
- **" I'm not breaking rules" is a weak defense**. Rules are often minimums, not maximums. For example, " no loud music after 10pm" is a rule, but " no bass that rattles neighbors' windows at 3pm" might be an unwritten expectation. 
- **" I paid extra for the spot"**— but did the lease explicitly say " you can play music at any volume"? Unlikely. Mechanics spots are for * car work*, not * sound system testing*. 
- **" It's my car, my space"**— but in an apartment, " your space" is shared. The parking spot is common area, not private property. 
- **" I tried to accommodate"**— they did turn it down once, but when asked to adjust bass specifically ( which is the real issue), they didn't fully comply. " I'll try" isn't enough if the problem persists. 
- **" I used earbuds and it wasn't the same"**— that's on them. If they want to enjoy their system, they need to find a way that doesn't disturb others. 

**Key red flags**: 
- The neighbor's kids' room is being affected at 8:30pm ( before quiet hours start). That's a * real* disruption to a family's routine. 
- " Complaint after complaint" from management implies this isn't just one person being sensitive. 
- " R rattling walls" is a physical phenomenon— bass frequencies can travel through structures, and if it's causing that, it's objectively too loud for an shared living space. 

**What AITA would say**: 
- **YTA ( you're the asshole)**. 
- Why? Because " not breaking rules" is a cop-out. The * spirit* of the rules is about being considerate. If your bass rattles neighbors' walls and disrupts their sleep, that's not " reasonable noise"— it's a violation of basic community living. 
- The " mechanics spot" is for car work, not a free pass to blast bass. If they wanted to enjoy their system, they should have done it in a way that doesn't affect others ( e.g., at a driving range, on a closed track, or using headphones). 
- Management's request to use headphones is * reasonable*. If the system is " so important" to them, they can still enjoy it privately. 

**Additional angles**: 
- **Legal perspective**: Many cities have " noise ordinances" that prohibit " unreasonably loud noise" at any time, not just during quiet hours. Bass that rattles windows might violate those. 
- **Lease terms**: Most leases have clauses about " disturbing other tenants" even during daytime. 
- **Practical solution**: If they * must* work on the car with music, they could use a portable Bluetooth speaker at low volume, or better yet, headphones. 

**Final verdict**: 
- **YTA**. 
- They're not " r rude" because they're " within their rights"— they're being inconsiderate by prioritizing their hobby over others' peace. The fact that management is getting multiple complaints and specifically asked them to use headphones ( a simple, low-cost solution) means they're the problem here. 
- " I paid extra for the spot" doesn't mean " I can do whatever I want"— it means " I can work on my car here," not " I can turn this into a personal concert venue." 
- If they truly love their car, they'd find a way to enjoy it without being a nuisance. 

**Why not " NTA"?** 
- " I'm not breaking rules" is a common AITA defense, but it's almost always YTA if the behavior is objectively disruptive. Rules are baseline; common courtesy is the real standard. 
- " R rattling walls" is a clear sign of excessive noise. Even if it's before 10pm, that's not " normal" daytime noise. 
- The " I tried to accommodate" argument fails because they only partially complied ( turned down volume but not bass specifically) and then " cranked it to drown out his barking"— which is escalatory and unproductive. 

**Conclusion**: 
- **YTA**. 
- They need to respect their neighbors' right to a peaceful environment. Headphones are the solution. If they can't do that, they should find a different place to work on their car ( e.g., a public garage, a friend's property, or a dedicated car audio shop). 
- This isn't about " being an asshole"— it's about basic human decency in shared living spaces. 
- ( P.S. If they * really* want to enjoy their system, they should consider a driving range or a track day— not an apartment complex where people are trying to sleep or live their lives.)
